content.thinking:
I'm sorting out the left/right coordinate convention relative to the model's orientation, then deciding to stick with safer, simpler geometry primitives like sweeps, lathes, extrudes, and spheres rather than riskier constructs like surface loops, since I can't preview the renders directly.

Rather than cutting the mantle with a plane at each chain joint — which risks failure if a point sits inside the mesh — I'll switch to a circular (not elliptical) cross-section for the mantle so the ribs can be built as lathes around its centerline, using a shared radius function computed from the catmull path for consistency between the sweep and the lathes.

For glow strips along the flanks, I'm wary of using clock-angle placement since orientation isn't well defined; instead I plan to compute the strip path directly from my own geometry by offsetting the centerline points perpendicular to the tangent in the model's X direction.

Working out the dorsal/ventral basis vectors so I can place details at arbitrary angles around the mantle, deriving a formula pointOnMantle(t, φ, lift) using tangent-perpendicular vectors — though I'm second-guessing which direction counts as front versus back-down as I plug in the specific tangent values.

I don't need exact precision here — just a rough dorsal direction vector to drive the shading gradient. For the color layout, I'll go with mid-blue flanks and a light-cyan belly panel centered on the front, accented with orange chevrons, giving it that Overwatch-style color blocking.

For the tentacles, I'm mapping surface normals against world-up so the tops paint navy, sides blue, and the undersides cyan show through when the arms are raised. I'm defining a generic skin-paint function that takes an up vector and seam spacing, computing the angle between the normal and that up vector to decide top-versus-underside coloring and blending colors along seams.

Now I'm working out the exact seam logic and assembling the color palette -- navy, blue, cyan, cream, orange, gunmetal, and water tones -- to build out the gradient bands from dorsal to ventral surfaces.

I'll add darker panel seam lines in the flank region at ring spacing, and skip the chevron scale hint idea to keep things simple. For the gunmetal armor parts, I'll keep flat colors with bevel edges via extrusion to get that panel-line look.

Now I'm setting up specific coordinates, defining a root base joint, then lathing the water disc profile centered at the base with a slightly curved rim to give it thickness and a beveled edge.

I'm figuring out a radial ripple pattern for the water paint, computing distance from the disc's center to drive sine-wave ripples blended with noise for a natural texture. Writing paint shader logic...

Adding splash spike cones around the body...

I'll merge the droplet spheres into a single geometry using mergeGeometries for efficiency. For the skirt, I'm sketching a lathed dome profile with an outer wall flaring out to a lip and curving back to a thin inner wall, though I need to work out how it meets the arms.

Checking the math, the arms sit well below the skirt's bottom edge at each radial distance, so the skirt reads more like a flared collar or hood sitting above the arm roots rather than enclosing them—giving it an armored mantle look.

I think I'm overcomplicating the skirt geometry; I should simplify by dropping it and letting the arm roots blend directly into the head. But checking the azimuth spacing, eight arms at that radius overlap heavily into a cramped cluster, so I need to push the root ring outward to around 0.95 to give them breathing room.

Even at the larger radius the arms still crowd together, so I'm shrinking the arm root radius and the two feeding tentacles separately to fit everyone around the ring with just enough gap for a web-like pattern. The real problem is the beak position: at the front azimuths the arm roots leave almost no clearance, so I need to lift the beak above the arm root ring instead of placing it at the same height.

Checking the arm spacing with narrower beak width works, so I'm testing angles for each arm pair around the body—34°, 62°, feed point at 90°, then mirroring to 118° and 148°—to make sure they distribute evenly without excessive overlap in the back region.

I'm also verifying arm root placement against the head ellipsoid to confirm the joints sit inside the head geometry rather than poking out.

Checking the mantle base geometry: starting the center at y=1.35 with radius 0.95 creates a bulb extending down to y=0.4, so I need arms to emerge from the bulb's surface around y=1.5 to blend naturally like an octopus, though the exposed bulb bottom below the arms might need extra mass to look right.

Adjusting so the creature reads as rising out of water - mantle radius 0.85 starting at y=1.55, bulb bottom at y=0.7, with arms dropping from y1.5 down to 1.0 as they spread outward, overlapping the bulb nicely. For the head I'm placing an ellipsoid centered at (0,1.95,0.55) with radii (1.0,0.88,0.95), and checking that eye spheres (radius 0.4, centered at ±0.86, 2.15, 0.78) sit properly embedded in the head surface with some protrusion outward to x≈1.26.

Now I'm working out the eye direction vector so the gaze points slightly forward and outward, then positioning an iris decal on the eyeball surface along that direction. I'm deciding on a dark gunmetal/navy eyeball color with a glowing amber iris and black slit pupil for that kraken-eye look, plus a gunmetal torus rim around the base of each eye for definition.

I'm noting the bezel overlaps the head slightly but that's fine, then moving on to the brows -- I want angled plate shapes above each eye for an angry look, swept along a curve starting from between the eyes.

Calculating brow path points...

Still refining the brow sweep path...

Now I'm thinking through the azimuth/elevation convention for positioning, where azimuth 0 points toward +Z and 90 toward +X, measured relative to the mesh's bounding box center. For head markings, I'm adding an orange accent chevron to the paint pattern, conditioning it on surface position and normal to target the forehead area.

Actually, I'll abandon the chevron painting approach on the head and instead sculpt real geometry: a swept-back crest plate running from the forehead back over the top of the head, defined as a polygon outline in the side profile plane.

This is getting too messy though — the base of the plate needs to follow the curved head and mantle surface, which is hard to anchor cleanly, so I'll drop the crest idea entirely.

Instead, maybe a membrane crest following the dorsal line of the mantle is more robust, using a chain of points swept with a defined direction vector, anchored to the mantle as the bone. Alternatively, a series of tapered dorsal armor spikes could work as a simpler substitute.

Designing blade-fin shapes...

Positioning the outline relative to the surface point rather than centreline, offsetting the quadrilateral coordinates by the local radius so each blade sits flush against the body. I'm leaning toward gunmetal-light fins with maybe a thin orange glow sweep along the edge for contrast.

Still shaping the lateral fins...

I'm reconsidering the fin orientation—since the fin plane spans the lateral and axial directions, viewed from the front it might look too thin as a flat wafer, so I'm thinking about angling the fins upward like wings to make them more visible.

Working out the thickness direction cross product confirms it points along P, good for the fin hinge setup. Now I'm setting up the fin joints with their hinge directions and positions along the chain, then starting to lay out the mantle's path points for its joint chain.

I'm estimating the overall mantle height and tentacle tip extension, then working out the mantle radius profile with keyframed values at several t positions to shape its taper from base to tip.

I'm leaning toward a bulbous teardrop mantle rather than a sharp squid point, smoothing the radius curve between keys with interpolation, and placing lathe rib rings at specific t values along with a collar band that includes a glowing gunmetal accent.

Defining rib and collar geometry...

I'm similarly working out polygon side counts for the tentacle cuffs, balancing low-poly facets against a smoother look, and leaning toward 8 sides for tentacles and 12 for the mantle so the ring radii stay safely outside the vertex radii.

For the tentacles I'm settling on 10-sided sweeps, with each arm segmented into roughly 40-60 bending rings to approximate the curvature, giving around 1000 triangles per arm. Now I'm sketching the beak geometry, placing the mouth center and defining bezier control points for the upper beak so it curves forward and down from the head toward a tilted-down tip.

Writing beak taper and color bands...

Settling on conservative curve coordinates for both beak parts so the upper hooks downward and the lower tucks under, keeping them close but not overlapping at rest.

I'll apply a slight jaw rotation of about 12 degrees around the X axis to open the mouth a bit, then check how the beak position lines up relative to the arm roots on the body.

Checking clearance against the head's lower front profile, the beak base sits comfortably inside the head's ellipsoid boundary at that height, with the tip extending just past it, which seems fine geometrically.

For the lower jaw, I'm verifying it stays buried within the head volume at its attachment point, then keeping things simple by skipping extra details like a jaw plate, mouth interior sphere, or beak lip ring, just assigning the upper beak to the head bone and the lower jaw to its own bone.

Now I'm working out the horns sweeping back from the brow sides, calculating the surface hit point using azimuth and elevation angles on the head ellipsoid, then plotting a bezier curve through control points out to the horn tip.

I'm checking whether the horn tip might collide with the fin, so I'm shrinking the horn's reach and recalculating its position relative to the mantle's surface to keep clearance.

Now I'm defining the horns with explicit absolute points, verifying the base point sits just inside the head ellipsoid, then plotting a bezier path from that base outward and upward with a tapering radius.

Still checking horn-mantle collisions, I push the horn path further outward to clear the mantle surface, verifying distances at each control point against the mantle radius, then start cross-checking the horn tip position against the fin plane to avoid overlap there too.

Still checking for clipping between the fins and horns, so I'm shortening the horn tips to end lower (around y=3.5) and nudging the fin placement up slightly to keep clear separation between the two features.

Then I'm checking the raised arms, feeding tentacles, and arch-curve arms for clearance against the fins and body at various angles — all positions look fine with reasonable gaps, so I'm moving on to verify the front-view silhouette with the lying arms extended outward.

Now I'm working out the arm coordinate conversion formula, deriving position vectors from the angle, radial distance, height, and lateral offset using direction and side vectors, and checking the sign symmetry between left and right sides.

Writing arm point coordinates...

Checking that the arm's reach stays within the water radius and verifying the floating height at a sample point along the curve looks right.

Now I'm plotting the arch path for the second arm, tracing through its control points until the tip ends in the water, and confirming the tip radius clears the surface. Then I start sketching the feeding gesture's root position for the third arm.

Still working out tentacle curl coordinates...

I'm computing root positions for each back arm based on angle offsets, then checking that these roots sit properly against the mantle bulb's surface so the sweep chains start cleanly.

I'm setting up the joint naming scheme for each arm segment, defining a radius taper function from thick root to thin tip for the sweep geometry, and placing sucker positions along the belly-facing side of raised arms using angular offsets from the body's centerline.

Now I'm scaling the sucker cup geometry relative to the tube's radius at each point, defining a lathe outline for the cups that tapers inward at the base and flares slightly outward.

The order traces counterclockwise, which should be fine for the lathe profile, and I'm checking for self-intersections which seem absent. I'm also verifying the curvature math works out given the buried base and mild tube radius, then moving on to counting parts.

With 10 arms × 9 cups, that's 90 cups total, feeding tentacle-like placement along the club section only. I'm settling on a cream color for the cups without any glow effect, and deciding to skip an accent rim to keep things simple. For cuffs, I'm picking four manual positions along each arm and working out how to pass the frame as a point input for the lathe axis and origin.

For the tip glow, I'm placing a small orange sphere near the tentacle end using a bone derived from the arm's path point, with bead radius around 0.07-0.09. I'm also adding glowing cuff rings along the arms for visual interest, then defining the feeding tentacle club's radius profile—tapering the stalk, bulging into the club shape, then narrowing again at the tip.

For the club, I'm using a sine-based bulge function layered on the tapering base radius, adding sucker cups in rows along the club surface, plus cuff rings and a glow band, and considering a small curved hook at the very tip.

Adding sweep geometry...

Now I'm thinking about seam placement for the arm ring joins, and considering whether to add chevron banding on the belly region or use a scales-based paint to create cell-outline plate textures on the flank for a cobbled look.

I'm weighing noise mottling against keeping things clean—deciding to skip texture noise and instead rely on gradient, seam lines, and accent dashes, like small orange dots spaced along the flank accent line for subtle plating detail.

Now I'm writing the SVG for the eye decal, using a radial gradient from yellow to orange to deep red with a dark stroke outline...

Confirming glow works on decal parts, then thinking about whether to add bioluminescent nodes along the mantle flank—deciding against separate parts in favor of painted dashes, and working out the orientation vectors needed to position accent lines along the curving dorsal line of the mantle.

Rather than computing an expensive per-texel closest-point lookup along the mantle path to align glow lines with the paint exactly, I'm opting to just use a fixed approximate up-vector for both the paint and the glow lines so they stay roughly consistent without the performance cost.

I realize the flanks (pure ±X sides) are special: there the angle from U is always 90° regardless of tilt, since the normal has no component along U there. So I can anchor the glow strips exactly at the ±X sides and redefine the paint's colour zones in terms of this same angular measure, making the dorsal band correspond to angles below roughly 40°.

This is getting too fiddly with exact normal-vector math — maybe it's simpler to just compute the mantle's local tangent directly from the path by sampling the closest point and using the path's own tangent function, rather than trying to approximate the front-facing direction analytically.
